title: Samut Sakhon Day Trip: Mahachai, Tha Chalom & Seafood
metaDesc: A morning-to-evening Samut Sakhon day trip from Bangkok: walk Mahachai market, take the 3-baht ferry to Tha Chalom, visit Wat Chong Lom, and eat fresh seafood on the Tha Chin River. With times, prices and honest tips.

h1:
Samut Sakhon in a Day
Mahachai, Tha Chalom & Seafood
intro: Samut Sakhon sits only about 30 kilometres from Bangkok — an hour's drive and you're there — yet plenty of people pass it on the highway without ever stopping. That's a shame, because the town of Mahachai has a fresh seafood market right on the Tha Chin River, a little ferry that carries you across to Tha Chalom for 3 baht (the old community that was Thailand's first provincial sanitary district), and Wat Chong Lom out at the river mouth where the breeze never stops. Here's a one-day plan we've put together so you can walk at an easy pace, eat your fill of seafood, and skip the overnight stay.

blocks.html: A one-day Samut Sakhon trip works any day of the week — Mahachai market, the ferry and the temples are all open daily, so you don't have to lock in a specific day the way you do with floating markets elsewhere. That said, if you want the freshest catch and a lively market, go in the morning: the fishing boats come in from before dawn through to mid-morning, so the seafood is fresher and there's more to choose from than in the afternoon. The charm of this place is that it's a real working town, not a set dressed up for tourists — so come without expecting everything polished, and you'll get the genuine river-mouth way of life instead.

blocks.text: A One-Day Plan, Morning to Evening

blocks.html: Leave Bangkok around 7am, take Rama II Road for roughly 30–35 kilometres, and you'll reach the centre of Mahachai. We've timed this so you start at Mahachai market while the catch is still fresh, then take the ferry across to Tha Chalom mid-morning, and finish with a riverside seafood lunch at noon plus Wat Chong Lom for the cool breeze in the afternoon.

blocks.label: Morning
blocks.title: Mahachai Market — Fresh Seafood on the Tha Chin River

items.activity: Leave Bangkok, drive Rama II Road toward Mahachai
items.note: About 30–35 km, roughly an hour. Allow extra time for morning traffic on Rama II.

items.activity: Arrive in central Mahachai, park near the market or Mahachai railway station, then walk into the market
items.note: There's parking at shophouses and town lots, around 20–40 baht. The market is right beside the Tha Chin River.

items.activity: Walk Mahachai market — check out the prawns, shellfish, crab and short mackerel just off the boats
items.note: It's one of the largest river-mouth seafood markets in Thailand, and cheaper than Bangkok. You can buy a foam box packed with ice to take home.

items.activity: Stop for breakfast in the market — fish congee, fish-ball noodles, or old-style coffee
items.note: Mahachai is known for its fish balls — springy because they use fresh sea fish. Order a small bowl to line your stomach before you keep walking.

items.activity: Walk to Mahachai pier on the Tha Chin River, ready to take the ferry across
items.note: The pier is close to the market and Mahachai railway station, just a few minutes' walk from the market.

blocks.title: Tip on buying seafood to take home
blocks.html: If you mean to take seafood back with you, buy it near the end of the day, not first thing in the morning when you'd be carrying it around for hours. Many stalls have foam boxes and ice to pack it. Tell the vendor how many hours you'll be travelling and they'll pack in enough ice — and always ask the price before they weigh it so there are no surprises when you pay.

blocks.label: Late Morning–Noon
blocks.title: Ferry to Tha Chalom + Wat Chong Lom

items.activity: Take the ferry from Mahachai across the Tha Chin River to Tha Chalom
items.note: The fare is 3 baht per person, the boat runs around the clock 24 hours, and the crossing takes only a few minutes. You can bring a motorbike or bicycle across too.

items.activity: Wander the old Tha Chalom community — old shophouse rows and riverside lanes
items.note: Tha Chalom was the site of Thailand's first provincial sanitary district (1905). The old buildings and the fishing-community way of life are still here.

items.activity: Visit Wat Suttiwat Wararam (Wat Chong Lom) at the river mouth — pay your respects and take in the view where the river meets the sea
items.note: The temple stands right at the mouth of the Samut Sakhon estuary, with a statue of King Rama V. A cool breeze blows constantly — that's where the name 'Chong Lom' (wind passage) comes from. It's a lovely spot to photograph the river mouth.

items.activity: Have a seafood lunch by the Tha Chin River around Tha Chalom, or head back to the Mahachai side
items.note: Plenty of riverside restaurants serve egg-laden crab, grilled prawns and steamed sea bass with lime — fresh, because they're right by the source.

blocks.title: Tip on the Mae Klong railway line
blocks.html: If you're not driving yourself, another fun option is the Mae Klong railway line from Wongwian Yai station down to Mahachai (about 31 km). There's no rail link between Mahachai and the Ban Laem side, so you get off, take the Tha Chin ferry across, and catch another train on to Mae Klong. Train lovers often pair this trip with Samut Songkhram in a single day.

blocks.text: Seafood You Shouldn't Miss on This Trip

blocks.html: Samut Sakhon is a genuine river-mouth seafood town, and the catch here stands out for being fresh and well-priced because it's right next to the fishing grounds and the wholesale market. These are the dishes we think are best value if you've only got a single day.

items.name: Mae Klong–Mahachai short mackerel (pla thu)
items.blurb: Short, fatty estuary mackerel, fried crisp outside and tender inside, eaten with shrimp-paste chilli dip and fresh vegetables. It's so iconic that Samut Sakhon has a mackerel roundabout as the town's symbol.

items.name: Steamed egg crab / blue swimmer crab
items.blurb: Firm-fleshed estuary crab, steamed hot and pulled apart to dip in punchy seafood sauce. Fresh off the boat, and better value than buying it in the city.
items.meta: Lunch · riverside restaurants · price by crab size

items.name: Grilled prawns
items.blurb: Big prawns grilled over charcoal — sweet, rich and easy to peel, dipped in seafood sauce. It's the dish people who come for Mahachai seafood usually order alongside the crab.
items.meta: Lunch · riverside restaurants · price by prawn size

items.name: Mahachai fish balls
items.blurb: Springy fish balls made from fresh sea fish, eaten in noodle soup or blanched with a dip. They're a local specialty, and a lot of people buy them to take home as a gift too.
items.meta: Breakfast–lunch · in the market · from a few dozen baht a bowl

items.name: Blanched cockles
items.blurb: Big estuary cockles, blanched just to the right point so the flesh stays soft and juicy, dipped in seafood sauce. An easy riverside snack you can find fresh around here.

items.name: Steamed sea bass with lime
items.blurb: A large sea bass steamed in lime, chilli and garlic — sour, spicy and balanced, with firm flesh. A shareable centrepiece for the whole table.

items.name: Fish or prawn congee
items.blurb: A seaside-town breakfast — clear broth with fresh fish or prawns, eaten warm in the morning before you walk the market. Light on the stomach and you taste how fresh the seafood is.

blocks.text: If You Have Time to Spare, Where Else to Stop

items.name: Mackerel Roundabout
items.blurb: The roundabout in central Mahachai with a mackerel statue as the province's symbol. A quick photo check-in as you drive past.

items.name: Phan Thai Norasing Shrine
items.blurb: A shrine and historical park telling the story of Phan Thai Norasing, who upheld the law. It's out of town toward Khlong Khok Kham — a good stop if you have time in the afternoon.

items.name: Ban Laem–Khok Kham salt fields
items.blurb: Roadside salt-evaporation fields along the Khok Kham–Ban Laem stretch, beautiful in the late afternoon light when the water turns to a mirror. A great way to close the trip with the sunset.

items: Private car — from Bangkok, take Rama II Road for about 30–35 km. The easiest option if you plan to buy seafood to take home and want to stop at several places.
Mae Klong railway line — ride from Wongwian Yai station down to Mahachai, about 31 km. An old-world atmosphere, ideal for train lovers who aren't in a hurry.
Mahachai–Tha Chalom ferry — the fare is 3 baht per person, running 24 hours a day, and you can bring a motorbike or bicycle across.
Parking — park on the Mahachai side near the market or railway station and explore on foot. If you're crossing to Tha Chalom without the car, the ferry is the easier way.

faq.q: Which day should I go for a Samut Sakhon day trip?
faq.a: Any day works, because Mahachai market, the ferry and the temples are all open daily — you don't have to lock in a specific day the way you do with floating markets elsewhere. But if you want the freshest catch and a lively market, go in the morning, since the fishing boats come in from before dawn through to mid-morning, so the seafood is fresher and there's more to choose from than in the afternoon.

faq.q: How much is the Mahachai–Tha Chalom ferry?
faq.a: The fare is just 3 baht per person. The boat crosses the Tha Chin River around the clock, 24 hours a day, the crossing takes only a few minutes, and you can bring a motorbike or bicycle across too. The pier is close to Mahachai market and the railway station.

faq.q: Where's the best place to buy seafood in Samut Sakhon?
faq.a: Mahachai market on the Tha Chin River is one of the largest river-mouth seafood markets in Thailand, with fresh prawns, shellfish, crab and short mackerel at lower prices than in Bangkok. Buy it near the end of your visit and ask the vendor to pack a foam box with enough ice for your journey.

faq.q: What's interesting about Wat Chong Lom in Tha Chalom?
faq.a: Wat Suttiwat Wararam, or Wat Chong Lom, is a royal temple right at the mouth of the Samut Sakhon estuary, with a statue of King Rama V. A cool sea breeze blows all day long — that's where the name 'Chong Lom' (wind passage) comes from. The riverside spot in front of the temple is a beautiful place to watch the Tha Chin River flow out to sea.

faq.q: Is one day enough for Samut Sakhon, or should I stay overnight?
faq.a: A there-and-back day trip is very doable, since it's only about 30 kilometres from Bangkok — an hour's drive. If you'd rather take it slower, or you want to see the salt fields at sunset and wake up to walk the market in the morning, an overnight in Mahachai adds a little more atmosphere.
